analysis.one_liner: Bans agencies from issuing a new regulation unless they repeal three existing ones first.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop any federal agency from issuing a new rule that imposes costs on businesses or state and local governments unless it first repeals three existing related rules. For 'major' rules — those with roughly $100 million or more in annual economic impact — the new rule's cost would also have to be certified as no greater than the cost of the rules repealed. It would also require every agency to report to Congress on which of its rules are costly, ineffective, duplicative, or outdated.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that face federal regulation gain the most: the bill makes it structurally hard for agencies to issue new consumer, worker, environmental, and financial protections, since each one requires clearing out three old rules and balancing costs. Regulated industries — from polluters to banks to drug makers — benefit from slower, thinner rulemaking.

how_it_helps.text: Blocks agencies from issuing any new rule that costs businesses, nonprofits, or state and local governments money unless they first repeal three related existing rules.

For major rules — those with an annual economic effect of at least $100 million or significant effects on prices, competition, employment, or investment — the new rule's cost must be certified by OIRA as less than or equal to the cost of the rules repealed.
Requires every agency, within 90 days of enactment, to submit a report identifying each of its rules as costly, ineffective, duplicative, or outdated.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost through weaker or slower public protections: pollution controls, workplace safety, consumer finance, food and drug safety, and other safeguards would become far harder to issue or update, because agencies must clear three repeals and a cost-balancing test before acting. Agencies and state and local governments also lose the ability to adapt rules to new problems.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary people relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The one-in-three-out requirement treats all rules as interchangeable, allowing a significant new public-health or safety rule to be blocked by the difficulty of finding three old rules to repeal, regardless of the benefits the new rule would deliver.
The cost cap for major rules ignores benefits entirely: a rule with very high benefits but a higher cost than the rules it replaces could not be certified or issued.

Supporters argue agencies accumulate outdated and duplicative rules and that a forced purge improves regulatory quality; opponents counter that laws like the Clean Air Act are updated through new rules, and freezing rulemaking leaves old standards in place as conditions change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For businesses, the benefit is fewer and weaker new regulations. For the public, the cost is real: agency rules are the main way federal law is kept current on safety, health, and consumer protection, and this bill makes the entire pipeline much slower and, for major rules, nearly conditional on a cost cap that excludes benefits. The bill would substantially impair the government's ability to respond to new hazards, which is a serious cost even for people who agree some rules are outdated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary committees with no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the Congress ended before it moved.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 14, 2025, by Rep. Stephanie Bice and referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, and in addition to the House Judiciary Committee.
No further action was taken: it never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or a vote in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regulated industries are better off because the bill died: the rulemaking pipeline that produces new consumer, worker, and environmental protections remains unchanged. Agencies also retain their ability to update or repeal rules on their own judgment rather than under a forced three-for-one and cost-cap formula.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries; agencies keep rulemaking discretion

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans introduced or cosponsored the bill (24 Republican cosponsors); no Democrats were involved, and the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, and others)
industries.note: The bill would make it much harder for agencies to issue new rules imposing costs or compliance duties on them, slowing or blocking new consumer, worker, and environmental requirements. Industry benefits from weaker regulation even when the public loses protection.

Agencies would be constrained by the three-for-one rule and the cost cap, and would face a new reporting requirement to identify their rules as costly, ineffective, duplicative, or outdated. Some agency internal and procurement rules are exempt.

analysis.trajectory: Dead; the Congress has ended, so no further action is expected.
